newsitem.title: FRANCE: France prepares new Corsica crackdown.
newsitem.headline: France prepares new Corsica crackdown.

text.p: The French government was set to launch a crackdown on militant Corsican separatists on Tuesday after a bomb attack on Prime Minister Alain Juppe's Bordeaux mayoral office signaled the end of secret peace talks.

In a tough statement on Monday night, Juppe equated Corsican guerrillas with Algerian Moslem fundamentalists, saying the government would "fight this terrorism with the same vigour it showed in combating other forms of terrorism last year".

Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre vowed on Tuesday to lock up more separatists of the Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC), which planted Saturday's highly symbolic bomb in Bordeaux, causing damage but no casualties.
Citing evidence that the militants were planning to step up violence in mainland France, Debre deployed armed riot police to guard public buildings in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux.

Political analysts said the FLNC's hardline Historic Wing had provoked a confrontation with Paris by targeting Juppe, launching a new escalation in the cycle of violence and repression that has marked the 21-year-old Corsican separatist movement.
The Bordeaux bomb gave the authorities a pretext for a roundup of armed activists that would have widespread support not only on the mainland but also on the Mediterranean island.
Polls show a big majority of Corsicans, while sympathetic to some autonomist ideas, are fed up with the violence and the harm it has done to the local economy.

"What the (Historic Wing) is doing now is even more suicidal than what they have done so far. They would do better to get back into line because this will lead nowhere," said Gilbert Casanova, president of the Ajaccio chamber of commerce.
Debre said police had already arrested 22 Corsican militants suspected of direct or indirect involvement in bombings and seized large quantities of weapons.
"We don't make speeches, we take action," he said. "Dialogue cannot work unless public order is restored."
Most commentators said the Bordeaux attack was a sign of weakness and isolation of the most militant Corsican separatists rather than of their strength.
But they still have several hundred armed followers, with a huge supply of weapons and explosives hidden in Corsica's maquis highlands as well and a network of supporters on the mainland.

"They have farmhouses with arms caches and significant stocks of dynamite in Provence (southern France). They have "sleeper" commando cells there which can be activated, with well trained motorcyclists capable of planting several explosive devices in a single night," said Roland Jacquard, head of the International Terrorism Observatory with good police sources.

Guy Benamou, Corsica expert of Liberation daily, said the Historic Wing had "declared a war it has no chance of winning. But it no doubt preferred to save its honour by going down to a military defeat rather than admit its political defeat."

The FLNC failed to win its key demands in secret talks with government emissaries who offered economic aid, a political role and an amnesty for separatists who turned in their guns, but rejected any change in Corsica's constitutional status, cabinet sources said.
The negotiations split the separatists, fuelling tit-for-tat killings between rival groups.
The most spectacular blow in that vendetta, a car bomb that killed one Historic Wing leader and seriously injured another in July, scared off tourists and ruined the summer season.

The FLNC has long been taken less seriously than the Irish Republican Army (IRA) fighting British rule in Northern Ireland or Basque ETA guerrillas in Spain because it has confined its actions to Corsica and rarely spilled blood.
There have been more than 80 bomb attacks on government offices and police stations in Corsica since July, but Saturday's was only the second for many years on the mainland.
